newsitem.title: UK: Some carriers look for ex-UK air cargo rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Some carriers look for ex-UK air cargo rate rise.

text.p: Some airlines are optimistic that once the seasonal lull ends, air cargo traffic from the UK will pick up offering opportunities for sprintime rate increases, a Reuter survey shows.
This optimism is tinged with the realisation that in many cases these will only replace jet fuel surcharges introduced in October and November. But this optimism is not uniform.
Many airlines surveyed said a strong final quarter enabled them to meet 1996 targets on most if not all ex-UK routes.

"We are quite buoyant about 1997's prospects. Bearing in mind we are in the Christmas aftermath and companies have only just gone back to work, our business is not too bad at the moment and we expect it will soon get much better," said Emirates' UK and Ireland cargo manager Ray Dissan.

"I think it will be a good year for the UK air cargo industry," he said, adding that although sterling is currently very strong. British exports went through a last quarter 1996 boom and this is continuing".
Cathay Pacific's UK cargo sales executive James Gilliard said "1996 was excellent for us and we are hoping that this trend will continue".

"Certainly, immediately after Christmas, business dropped off but it has already picked up. From Britain, we are moving lots of cargo required for Hong Kong's new Chep Lap Kok airport and right now our flights are often choc-a-bloc full," he added.

Korean Air Lines ' UK cargo sales manager Frank Smith said Britain had been the carrier's only major European cargo station to perform above budget last year and he was confident of keeping up this momentum.

"Investment by Korean companies in the UK is growing because labour costs here are now lower than in Korea," noted Smith adding that "this bodes well for Korean Air Cargo in the UK in 1997. I can see a spring rate increase coming and getting more capacity," he said.

British airfreight wholesaler Air Menzies International (AMI) also had a good 1996, especially in the Far East and its general manager (commercial) Sharon Wright said "I can't see business slackening off...I think we will see very healthy growth this year, especially to the Far East."
But she warned carriers not to raise their hopes too highly about a round of spring rate rises.

"Whatever way one looks at the situation, the October fuel surcharges were rate increases to a customer like ourselves. If carriers tried to push them up again, we would be very unhappy," said Wright.
"Going into Chinese New Year, things are going particularly well for Singapore," she noted.

Emirates' Dissan agreed. "Usually, our (ex-UK) business to Singapore peaks in October and then dips. This last time around that didn't happen -- business went up in November and again in Deecember and I can't see this trend changing," he said.

Although lower rates can be obtained from transhipment carriers such as Thai International and Royal Brunei, the average on this route is 1.29 stg per kg for a 100 kg shipment -- about the same as in the peak October/November period.

Rates to Hong Kong have dropped sightly since in the last month. Cathay Pacific sources in the territory are nevertheless hinting that the five UK pence per kg fuel surcharge currently in force on the UK-HK route will be converted into an official rate rise in the spring. Cathay upped its ex-Hong Kong rates by HK$1.50 per kilo from Jan one.

Cathay's Gilliard said ex-UK prospects in the shorter term are good. although China's takeover of Hong Kong sovereignty in six months represents "an obvious area of undertainty" for the air cargo industry,
Cathay's new summer schedule, which will come into effect in April, may see more cargo capacity offered on new passenger frequencies.
But some industry sources said where some shippers had been able to take advantage of the slack market to obtain large discounts from carriers flying from London with a low payload to Hong Kong.

From London to Tokyo, the average rate has also fallen, despite around three percent rate increases introduced on the route by Japanese carriers from January 1 to belatedly cover the surge in jet fuel costs.
This is due to increased rate competition from non-direct carriers coupled with off-season lack of demand.
"We finished off 1996 very busy but the start of the new year has been very quiet," said All Nippon Airways' ' assistant UK cargo manager John O'Shea.
"It is to early to speculate on whether or not there will be another cargo rate increase in the spring," he said.
Another dip in rates is seen from London to Seoul, to 2.02 stg from 2.05 stg per kg for 100 kgs, but Korean Air's Frank Smith is confident that they will soon go up.
Europe's economic outlook and competition from Lufthansa's and Air France's are key factors, but there is a possibility we will be able to raise rates in the spring, KAL's Smith said.
"All the Korean investment going on in Britain has given London the go-ahead over Milan for a second weekly 747 freighter service to Seoul, probably starting in mid summer," he said.
The current low season has seen a five pence fall to 2.14 stg in the average ex-London per kg tariff to Australia, but again industry hopes are high for a recovery.
"We are looking for 15 percent growth in tonnage and revenue from the UK to Australia this year," said wholesaler AMI's Wright.
Emirates' Dissan said that his carrier's Dubai-Melbourne Boeing 777 service, launched on a three-times-weekly basis last July, was proving to be very successful.
It is fed with cargo by all of the airline's worldwide stations and he predicted Emirates' share of the airfreight market to Australia would grow during 1997.
As for the Middle East, Dissan speculated that an ex-UK rate increase would be implemented by Emirates from Britain to Dubai from April 1.
"Why not? We are always looking to increase revenues to cover our costs, which have risen sharply over recent months," he said.

Dissan did not think the start of the Islamic month of Ramadan in mid-January would have too much of an adverse affect on his business. "There is always a slowdown at this time but it can hardly be compared with, for example, Chinese New Year when everything closes down in the main countries where it is celebrated," he said.

But Gil Harding, managing director of DAS Air Cargo's management company, London Gatwick-based ANA Aviation Services, disagreed, saying that Ramadan would represent "a major downturn in business" for his carrier.

DAS Air currently operates two weekly London-Dubai flights with a 65-tonne capacity DC-10 freighter. Rates on the route had dipped sharply of late mainly because of excessive competition but Harding is confident business would pick up after February.
ANA Aviation is also UK cargo sales agent for Air Gabon whose Gatwick-Libreville connects with onward flights to South Africa and Harding said this business is booming.

Average market rates on the route vary considerably, from 1.30 stg per kg charged by wholesalers to 1.50 stg quoted by Affretair, around 1.60 stg by Air Gabon, Air Namibia and Alitalia and between 1.80-1.90 by South African Airways and British Airways for direct high frequency services.
"We are looking for a rate increase from March 1," said Harding.
From the UK to Scandinavia, airlines have benefited over recent months as a result of the channel tunnel fire and the French truck drivers dispute.
Both had a tremendous impact on our traffic to Copenhagen and Sweden and we experienced four to six weeks of record tonnages, Scandinavian Airlines System's UK cargo manager Howard Jones said.
"SAS have showed what we can do on the airfreight side.in terms of service and reliability and now we will try our utmost to keep those customers. I don't see why we can't succeed," he stated.

Lufthansa cargo marketing manager in the UK Rudi Helm said it would continue its normal practice of increasing rates at the start of March and October. Details of increases have not been finalised but Helm expects Seoul, Hong Kong and Japan rates to rise along with Bombay where rates have lagged.

Lufthansa's express products now account for 13 percent of UK revenue with perhaps 55-60 percent of this going to Europe - mainly German destinations - on Boeing 737 QC (quick change) from Heathrow to Cologne and East Midlands to Frankfurt. The weight limit for Lufthansa's ex-UK cargo is normally 70 kilos but in practice it is usually loadability that is the constraining factor.
A pick-up in transatlantic traffic after the seasonal slow-down was also noted by Air Canada's UK and Ireland cargo sales manager Mike Judkins.

Features of Air Canada's recent ex-UK business have been transhipments to Canada of Israeli vegetables and of Dutch ones trucked to London. Another unusual cargo were a couple of large loads totalling 35 tonne for Boston which were flown from London but originated in Dublin, said Judkins. But he declined to detail this cargo adding that rates have not altered much since before Christmas despite the lower volume.
Howard Jones, of SAS, said: "Our ex-UK business to New York (Newark) and Chicago is still bubbling as we enter the new year and we are hopeful this will continue."
American Airlines' cargo manager John Smith stressed that business remains very quiet across the Atlantic although the carrier had already carried some good loads from the UK.

"Esssentially the whole industry has had two weeks holiday and manufacturing companies will not be looking to rebuild exports until after January 15...we are not looking for rate increase before spring," he said warning that the strength in sterling may be dangerous to British exports although current business levels remain good.

Iberia's Sagra said after a last minute pre-Christmas rush to get rid of a backlog of cargo destined for Latin America, business was now much quieter although oil industry cargoes are filling space to Mexico and Venezuela. A rate rise is likely in February or March, he added.
Alitalia northern Europe cargo manager Paul Rodwell said he doubts if rates to Latin America will rise soon and does not think surcharges will change into rate increases.
Last year Alitalia's ex-UK tonnage rose 7-8 percent in addition to an increase in yields, he added.
Likewise Paul Ryan at Brazil's Varig does not see rate increases replacing surcharges which when invoiced as a supplementary cost are clearer and avoid discounting.

UK truckers continue to impose a fuel surcharge of four to five pence a kilo and cargo industry sources expect these, as with air surcharges, to remain in force whilst energy prices stay high. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
